prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A grand piano wrapped in quilted pads by movers, tied up with canvas straps—like classical music’s birthday gift to the criminally insane—is gently nudged without its legs out an eighth-floor window on 62nd street. It dangles in April air from the neck of the movers’ crane, Chopin-shiny black lacquer squares and dirty white crisscross patterns hanging like the second-to-last note of a concerto played on the edge of the seat, the edge of tears, the edge of eight stories up going over—it's a piano being pushed out of a window and lowered down onto a flatbed truck!— and I’m trying to teach math in the building across the street. Who can teach when there are such lessons to be learned? All the greatest common factors are delivered by long-necked cranes and flatbed trucks or come through everything, even air. Like snow. See, snow falls for the first time every year, and every year my students rush to the window as if snow were more interesting than math, which, of course, it is. So please. Let me teach like a Steinway, spinning slowly in April air, so almost-falling, so hinderingly dangling from the neck of the movers’ crane. So on the edge of losing everything. Let me teach like the first snow, falling.

Keywords: April, Chopin, Who

outputs.L1:
A grand piano, wrapped by movers in quilted pads and bound with canvas straps—like classical music’s birthday gift to the criminally insane—is gently nudged, legless, through an eighth-floor window on 62nd Street. It dangles in the April air from the neck of the movers’ crane, its Chopin-shiny black lacquer squares and dirty-white crisscross patterns suspended like the second-to-last note of a concerto played on the edge of one’s seat, the edge of tears, the edge of going over from eight stories up. It’s a piano being pushed out of a window and lowered onto a flatbed truck!—and I’m trying to teach math in the building across the street.

Who can teach when there are such lessons to be learned? All the greatest common factors are delivered by long-necked cranes and flatbed trucks, or they come through everything, even air. Like snow.

See, snow falls for the first time every year, and every year my students rush to the window as if snow were more interesting than math—which, of course, it is.

So, please. Let me teach like a Steinway spinning slowly in the April air, so nearly falling, so precariously dangling from the neck of the movers’ crane. So on the edge of losing everything.

Let me teach like the first snow, falling.
outputs.L2:
Across from my classroom on East 62nd Street, movers ease a legless grand piano through an eighth-floor window. Wrapped in padded quilts and cinched with canvas belts, it resembles an extravagant present intended for dangerously unhinged recipients. Suspended from a crane in the mild April sky, the instrument turns slowly above the street. Its glossy black finish appears in patches between grimy white bands, while it hangs with the unbearable suspense of a concerto nearing its final note—balanced between anticipation and grief, eight floors above disaster. Yet this is no metaphor: a piano really is being guided out of a window and lowered toward a flatbed truck.

Meanwhile, I am supposed to be teaching mathematics in the building opposite. But how can anyone conduct a lesson when the world is offering a spectacle like this? The most important common factors arrive by crane and truck, or pass through everything around us, including the atmosphere. They come like snow. Each year, when the season’s first flakes descend, my students crowd around the windows as though snowfall matters more than mathematics—and naturally, it does.

So let me teach the way a Steinway hangs there: rotating gently in the April air, seeming always about to drop, awkwardly restrained by the crane’s long neck, poised at the brink of total loss. Let my teaching resemble the year’s first snow as it comes down.
outputs.L3:
Across the street, movers are carefully lowering a grand piano from an eighth-floor window with the help of a crane. Suspended high above the ground, the piano becomes a dramatic spectacle, and its slow, precarious descent distracts the speaker from teaching mathematics. Yet the interruption also offers a lesson of its own: profound insights do not always come from textbooks or formal instruction, but can emerge from ordinary events and the world around us.

The scene recalls the way students respond to the first snowfall of the year. No matter how carefully a lesson has been planned, their attention naturally turns toward the windows, captured by beauty, surprise, and wonder. Rather than resisting that instinct, the speaker longs to bring the same qualities into the classroom—to teach with the suspense of a piano hanging in midair and the beauty of freshly falling snow. In this vision, learning would become not merely an obligation, but something vivid, immediate, and impossible to ignore.
outputs.L4:
From an eighth-floor classroom window, a teacher watches movers lower a grand piano toward the street. Suspended by ropes high above the ground, the instrument seems at once majestic and fragile. Its dark, polished body hangs in the open air like an enormous bird, a ship drifting through the sky, or a question whose answer depends on the strength of a few narrow lines. The movers guide it carefully, while those watching hold their breath, aware that a single mistake could turn beauty into disaster.

The spectacle reminds the teacher of the first snowfall, when students abandon their mathematics lessons and rush toward the windows. Equations, fractions, and carefully prepared explanations suddenly lose their authority. Outside, snow transforms the ordinary world, and the students respond with immediate wonder. Their attention is not the result of discipline or obligation; it is freely given to something astonishing.

By linking the suspended piano with the students’ excitement, the poem reimagines what teaching might be. A true lesson should contain some of the same suspense, beauty, and vulnerability. It should make students pause, look closely, and feel that something important is at stake. Rather than presenting knowledge as fixed and lifeless, a teacher might allow ideas to appear precarious and surprising, like a grand piano floating between a high window and the street.

The poem therefore suggests that education is not confined to textbooks or classroom exercises. Experience itself can become a powerful teacher. A snowfall, a dangerous task, or an unexpected sight may awaken curiosity more effectively than formal instruction. The teacher’s challenge is not simply to deliver information, but to create conditions in which attention, wonder, and discovery become possible.
outputs.L5: In April, the rain played Chopin against the windows—soft nocturnes of silver and gray. I listened from the empty room and wondered who had left the piano open, who had placed lilacs on the table, who still remembered the melody we once called ours.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a math teacher distracted by movers lowering a grand piano from an eighth-floor window across the street.
counterfactuals.output:
At the board, Mr. Vale is dividing infinity  
into portions small enough for chalk.

He writes *x*, erases it, writes *x* again,  
while across the street eight floors of air  
hold a black grand piano by a rope.

The movers lean from the open window,  
their gloves bright as little flags.  
Slowly, the instrument descends—  
a polished nightfall, a silent whale  
lowered through the blue arithmetic of morning.

Mr. Vale turns from the theorem.

The class waits inside its rows of desks,  
thirty unfinished equations breathing softly.  
No one speaks. Even the clock seems caught  
between one second and the next.

The piano passes the seventh floor,  
the sixth. Sunlight travels along its lacquer  
like a hand remembering music.  
Its three legs point helplessly toward earth;  
its lid is closed upon all possible songs.

Mr. Vale still holds the chalk aloft.

He had meant to explain the limit:  
how something may approach forever  
and never arrive. But there, outside,  
the great dark body keeps arriving—  
past curtains, fire escapes, windows  
where strangers lift their faces.

At the third floor the rope shivers.

A gasp moves through the classroom  
as wind touches the piano  
and makes it turn, almost gracefully,  
above the traffic. For one suspended moment  
it belongs to no room, no recital,  
no sorrowing family. It is only weight  
dreaming it can float.

Then down again.

Mr. Vale lowers his hand.  
On the board, the unfinished proof  
gleams white and certain.

Across the street, the movers guide the piano  
into the waiting truck,  
and the whole class watches the darkness  
disappear inside darkness.

“Where were we?” he asks at last.

But no one answers.

Outside, the rope rises empty  
toward the eighth-floor window,  
a thin vertical line  
through which the morning  
has solved nothing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a Steinway dangling from a crane in Manhattan, using surreal metaphors and connecting the spectacle to teaching, snowfall, and the fear of losing everything.
counterfactuals.output:
A Steinway dangles above Manhattan like a black tooth pulled from the mouth of a giant, its lacquered body catching the windows in splinters. The crane’s cable is a single line of handwriting, and the piano hangs at the end of it like a lesson no teacher knows how to finish.

Below, taxis swarm like dropped yellow notes. Above, the sky begins rehearsing snow—one white key at a time—until the city seems covered in chalk dust from some enormous classroom. The piano turns slowly in the wind, a dark moon with pedals, while everyone on the sidewalk looks up as if waiting to be called on.

It is teaching them something without playing: how weight can become suspense, how beauty depends on a knot, how every possession is already practicing its disappearance. Each snowflake touches the Steinway and vanishes. Each person imagines the cable snapping—not only the instrument falling, but the apartment, the job, the names of loved ones, the whole careful music of a life dropping through the air.

Still, the piano hangs there, silent and impossible, holding all its songs inside it like a teacher holding back the answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph poem in the voice of a teacher who realizes that real-world wonder—a suspended piano, the season’s first snow—is more compelling than a lesson on greatest common factors.
counterfactuals.output: I had written twelve and eighteen on the board, chalked their factors into tidy rows, when outside the window a piano floated above the street, black and shining, held by a crane’s thin cable like a question no workbook dared to ask; then the first snow began, softening every roof and shoulder, and even the children who feared numbers pressed their faces to the glass. I set down the chalk. Let six be the answer another day. For now, we watched the impossible instrument sway through the white air, each flake finding its own brief place, and learned what cannot be divided.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine you are teaching math when a padded grand piano is pushed out of a nearby apartment window and lowered onto a truck. Turn the scene into an emotional meditation on how you wish you could teach.
counterfactuals.output:
Halfway through the proof, a grand piano appeared outside the window.

It came sideways, wrapped in quilted blue pads and cinched with ropes, as if the sky were lowering an enormous, sleeping animal. My students turned at once. Even the ones who had been hiding behind their hair looked up. The piano swung above the street, six stories from the pavement, while two movers leaned from the neighboring window and shouted instructions we could not hear.

I stopped talking.

On the board, I had written: **Given. Prove.** Between the two words stretched my careful ladder of reasons. But no one was looking at it now. We watched the piano descend by inches, tremble in the wind, knock softly against the brick, and continue toward the waiting truck.

I wanted to teach like that.

I wanted each lesson to arrive from an unexpected height, carrying the weight of something made to sing. I wanted mathematics to enter the room wrapped in mystery, visibly dangerous and tenderly protected. I wanted my students to feel that what we were handling mattered enough to require ropes, pulleys, shouted warnings, many hands.

Instead, I so often gave them numbers already unpacked. I placed formulas on their desks like flat furniture and asked them to assemble the correct answer. I told them which parts were important. I hurried them past bewilderment. When they struggled, I mistook their silence for absence, though perhaps they were only standing beneath something immense, unsure where it would land.

The piano turned slowly in the air. For one moment its shape became unmistakable beneath the blankets: the long body, the curved side, the delicate legs bound close. Someone in the back whispered, “How can the rope hold all that?”

There it was—the question I wished every class could begin with.

Not *What formula do we use?* Not *Will this be on the test?* But: How can this slender thing hold such weight? How do we know? What would happen if it failed? What invisible balance keeps disaster from becoming disaster?

I imagined abandoning the proof and asking them to estimate the piano’s mass, the tension in the ropes, the angle of the cable, the force of the wind. But even that seemed too small, too eager to convert wonder into work. So we simply watched.

The movers guided the piano down. One stood on the truck with both arms raised, not touching it yet, only ready. I recognized that gesture. It was what I wanted teaching to be: not dragging knowledge into students, not pushing from above, but standing near the place where something difficult and precious might arrive. Ready to steady it. Ready to keep it from striking the ground. Trusting, too, that its weight belonged to them.

When the piano finally settled onto the truck bed, the class exhaled together. For a few seconds, we were not quick students or slow students, not teacher and taught. We were witnesses to a problem the world had posed and, somehow, solved.

Then the truck pulled away.

I turned back to the board. **Given. Prove.**

The words looked lonelier than before. I picked up the eraser and wiped away the proof, rung by rung.

“Let’s start,” I said, “with what you noticed.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an exuberant, image-rich prose poem that begins with piano movers on East 62nd Street and ends with the speaker asking to teach like the first snow falling.
counterfactuals.output:
Piano movers on East 62nd Street shoulder a black grand  
through the blue astonishment of morning,  
its lacquered flank holding whole avenues in miniature—  
yellow cabs, awnings, the quick red scarves of strangers,  
a florist lifting buckets of tulips like brief, bright fires.  
The men call to one another in ropes and pulleys,  
in the hard grammar of weight,  
and the piano, mute emperor, rises inch by inch  
toward a window flung open six stories above.

What a city of impossible entrances!  
A cello descends into the subway.  
A baker shakes flour from his apron  
and becomes, for one radiant second, weather.  
Pigeons detonate from a cornice.  
Steam gallops white-maned from the grates,  
wreathing the knees of schoolchildren  
who carry their lunches like small locked gardens.

I walk east with my heart unbuttoned.  
The river is hammering silver into silver.  
On every pane the sun practices its signatures;  
on every fruit cart, oranges heap themselves  
into little planets eager for names.  
Even the sirens seem jubilant—  
red needles sewing distance to desire—  
and scaffolds climb the buildings  
with their iron vines and wooden blossoms.

Above me, the piano enters the sky.  
For an instant it hangs between street and room,  
between thunder and song,  
its three legs folded beneath it  
like a great dark bird remembering flight.  
I imagine all its sleeping music:  
waltzes curled in the felt,  
hymns tucked under the lid,  
one wild note pacing the keys  
like a tiger behind moon-white bars.

O morning, extravagant teacher,  
you write in exhaust and gold leaf,  
you erase with wind, begin again with bells.  
You place a coffee cup in a gloved hand  
and call it warmth; you toss a newspaper  
against a stoop and call it history;  
you lift a piano over traffic  
and call the whole trembling contraption faith.

I have been too careful with wonder,  
counting it like change, hiding it in drawers.  
Break me open into avenues.  
Let every face be a lit window,  
every sorrow a stairway carrying something upward.  
And when the roofs grow quiet, when the black branches  
hold out their empty palms to heaven,  
teach me to teach like the first snow falling?
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
